revision_note: Newly added with 8 verified chunks under public domain (2026-07-23, Batch 10). Source: Paul Carus's 1894 chapter 'Sariputta and Moggallana' for his conversion, and Henry Clarke Warren's 1896 Buddhism in Translations, section 41 'The Death of Moggallana' (translated from the Dhammapada and Buddhaghosa's commentary), fetched directly from sacred-texts.com etexts.

content.text: Moggallana was a Brahman and one of the chiefs of the followers of Sanjaya, leading a religious life together with his friend Sariputta. The two had made a solemn promise to each other: "He who first attains Nirvana shall tell the other one."
content.source_name: Paul Carus, The Gospel of Buddha (1894), ch. "Sariputta and Moggallana"

content.text: After Sariputta obtained the pure and spotless eye of truth through Assaji's teaching, he went to Moggallana and told him what he had learned. Both said: "We will go to the Blessed One, that he, the Blessed One, may be our teacher." When the Buddha saw the two friends coming from afar, he said to his disciples: "These two monks are highly auspicious," and when they had taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, he received them among his followers.
content.source_name: Paul Carus, The Gospel of Buddha (1894), ch. "Sariputta and Moggallana"

content.text: Of Moggallana the Buddha declared, as recorded in the Anguttara-Nikaya: "O priests, the chief of my disciples who possess magical power is Moggallana the Great." It was said that alms and honor flowed to the Buddha's community in no small part because Moggallana would visit the heavens and hells, question the beings reborn there about the karma that had shaped their fates, and report what he learned to men.
content.source_name: Henry Clarke Warren (trans.), Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana"

content.text: Rival ascetics, envious of the alms Moggallana's teaching brought the Buddha's community, hired highwaymen with a thousand pieces of money to kill him at Black Rock. The elder, perceiving he was surrounded, escaped through the keyhole; when they came again, he pierced the peaked roof and sprang into the sky. Neither during the early nor the middle part of the month could they capture him. But as the month drew to its close, held back at last by his own past karma, he could not flee, and the highwaymen captured him and broke his bones into bits the size of rice-grains, then left him for dead in a thicket.
content.source_name: Henry Clarke Warren (trans.), Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana"

content.text: The elder thought, "I will see The Teacher before I pass into Nirvana." Swathing himself about with meditation, as with a bandage, and thus stiffening his shattered body, he went to the Buddha by way of the air, did obeisance, and said: "Reverend Sir, I am about to pass into Nirvana." The Buddha asked from where, and bid him: "In that case, Moggallana, recite to me the Doctrine before you go: for I have no other such disciple as you." Moggallana rose into the sky, performed miracles, and recited the Doctrine; then, having again done obeisance to the Teacher, he returned to the forest of Black Rock and passed into Nirvana.
content.source_name: Henry Clarke Warren (trans.), Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana"

content.text: When priests in the lecture-hall said that Moggallana the Great had met a death unworthy of him, the Buddha replied: "Priests, the death of Moggallana the Great was unsuited to his present existence, but suited to his karma of a previous existence." He then told how, in a former birth, this same great soul, though otherwise devoted to his aged parents, had been provoked by his wife into staging a false robbery and killing them in the forest. "The fruit of this one deed of Moggallana's was torment in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, and death by pounding, in a hundred existences, as suited the nature of his crime."
content.source_name: Henry Clarke Warren (trans.), Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana"

content.text: King Ajatasattu dispatched spies who traced the murder to highwaymen hired by rival naked ascetics; he had five hundred of the ascetics and five hundred highwaymen executed. The Buddha taught that even a fully perfected disciple like Moggallana, foremost among the community in magical power and beloved by the Teacher above all others, was not exempt from the fruit of past karma -- a teaching preserved alongside the Dhammapada verses on the certain consequence of harming the innocent.
content.source_name: Henry Clarke Warren (trans.), Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana"

content.text: This entry compiles verified passages from two public-domain sources hosted on sacred-texts.com: Paul Carus's The Gospel of Buddha (Chicago: Open Court Publishing Co., 1894), ch. "Sariputta and Moggallana" (btg23.htm), for his conversion and ordination alongside Sariputta; and Henry Clarke Warren's Buddhism in Translations (Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 3, 1896), section 41 "The Death of Moggallana" (bits041.htm, translated from the Dhammapada and Buddhaghosa's commentary), for his epithet, his death by highwaymen, and the Buddha's karmic explanation. Both were fetched and quoted verbatim/near-verbatim; both predate the 1923 US public-domain cutoff. No other chapters about Moggallana were fetched this session, so additional legendary material (e.g. his contest of psychic powers with the naga king) is not represented here.
